part_title: Managed AI APIs and Amazon Comprehend Text Analysis
review_basis: Visually inspected all 29 original public/course-visuals/aif-course/module-08 numbered WebP images individually in order. Narration rewritten following exact diagram arrows, visible text/examples, numeric values, callouts, and exam comparisons, with product lifecycle caveats.

scenes.title: Why AWS AI Managed Services?
scenes.narration: Start at the upper left of the slide with the six kinds of input: text, speech, images, conversational intent, recommendations and enterprise search. Follow each horizontal arrow to the matching purpose-built AWS service. Text goes to Comprehend for insights or Translate for languages. Speech maps to Transcribe for audio to text or Polly for text to audio. Images go to Rekognition for visual analysis or Textract for extracting fields from documents. Conversation intent goes to Lex, user behavior to Personalize, and enterprise documents historically to Kendra. In the third and fourth columns the slide explains the output and a practical use case. Now look at the purple worked example below. An unhappy customer writes that resetting a password is frustrating. Comprehend detects negative sentiment, identifies key phrases such as reset password, and notes the English language. In the next blue example an invoice goes to Textract, which extracts invoice INV-1001, vendor ACME Ltd, invoice date 2024-01-15 and a total of 1,250 dollars. The green panel's decision is the key: choose a ready-made API for a defined task; if you need a custom machine learning model, evaluate SageMaker instead. Check: would Comprehend extract invoice table structure? No, Textract is the appropriate document service.

scenes.title: Amazon Comprehend
scenes.narration: Read the first row from left to right: a support email says, Delivery to Chennai was late, but support helped. That plain text enters Amazon Comprehend, which performs natural language processing rather than image recognition. The next panel illustrates three returned kinds of information: detected language English, location entity Chennai, key phrases delivery and support, and mixed sentiment. The CRM analyst dashboard organizes those signals, enabling a support team to see delivery problems and helpful support without reading every message. The upper results panel and the lower worked example are explicitly illustrative, not the exact JSON returned by an API. Now move to the lower middle: topic modeling groups a collection of support emails into themes such as delivery issues, support, refunds and product issues. That historical feature is closed to new Comprehend customers, so do not design a new integration without checking support. Finally compare Comprehend against Textract in the lower-right panel. Comprehend analyzes the meaning of text already available; Textract performs document OCR and extracts structure from scans. The practical test: for a scanned invoice, use Textract first if you need the text and fields, then optionally analyze that text.

scenes.title: Comprehend – Custom Classification
scenes.narration: This slide is a five-step process, so follow the numbered boxes across the top. One: store human-labeled support messages in Amazon S3, using categories such as billing and delivery. Two: train a custom Amazon Comprehend classifier from that data. Three: a new message arrives saying, I was charged twice for my order. Can you help me? Four: the trained model returns the class label billing. Five: the application routes the ticket to the Billing team. The lower worked example repeats this exact incoming message, classifier, predicted label and routing sequence. The point is that the model supplies a category, while application code performs the routing. Now compare the lower-right panel. Predefined Comprehend sentiment and entity APIs are ready-to-use general analysis tools. Custom classification instead learns organization-defined labels from your own examples. It does not guarantee the right answer on new input. Keep held-out labeled tickets for evaluation and check accuracy by category. Question: does finding a word such as Chennai within a ticket mean the entire ticket should be classified Chennai? No. Entity extraction detects spans; this model predicts a document category.

scenes.title: Named Entity Recognition (NER)
scenes.narration: Use the exact sentence in the upper-left panel: Maya met the team in Seattle on Tuesday. Notice the colored highlights: Maya in purple, Seattle in cyan and Tuesday in green. Follow the arrow into Amazon Comprehend and then to the identified entities table. The corresponding outputs are PERSON Maya, LOCATION Seattle, and DATE Tuesday. This is named entity recognition, or N E R. It identifies the location and type of a text span; it does not identify a person uniquely merely from a name. Now look at the lower two panels. Standard named entity recognition works out of the box for common types. Custom entity recognition can learn a company-specific type instead. The right-side example reads, The policy ACME-12345 was updated, and the trained recognizer extracts the value ACME-12345 under the custom label POLICY_ID. Both operations find pieces inside text rather than one class for an entire document. Check the type of output in an exam question: a category such as Billing points to classification, whereas the policy number or Seattle inside a sentence points to entity recognition.

scenes.title: Comprehend – Custom Entity Recognition
scenes.narration: Follow the longer arrow chain across the upper part of this slide. Start with labeled example documents in Amazon S3 and an entity label called POLICY_ID. Amazon Comprehend uses those examples to train a custom entity recognizer. A fresh customer message then arrives: Please review policy PL-2048. The trained recognizer processes that text and produces an extracted entity with type POLICY_ID and value PL-2048. The last green box represents a claims workflow that looks up the policy using that value. The model extracted an identifier; it did not decide whether a claim should be approved. In the lower-left worked example the sample policy document contains PL-2048 and a named customer, and the same identifier is detected from the new message. Compare the lower-middle panels: standard N E R detects generic people, locations and dates, while the custom recognizer detects a domain-defined policy number. The lower-right panel separates real-time analysis of one document from asynchronous batch analysis of many S3 documents. The useful decision is to train a custom recognizer when built-in entity types do not match your business schema. Check the labels and accuracy on new documents before trusting downstream automation.
